text:
In-Depth Analysis: Pagaya Technologies Ltd. 10-K/A Amendment – Key Investor Insights

Pagaya Technologies Ltd. Files Second Amendment to Annual Report: What Investors Need to Know

Pagaya Technologies Ltd. (Nasdaq: PGY) has filed its Second Amendment to its Annual Report on Form 10-K/A for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025. This filing is significant for investors as it provides updated disclosures and clarifications that may impact the company’s valuation and investor sentiment.

Key Highlights from the Amendment

Primary Purpose of the Amendment: The core update in this filing is an enhanced disclosure in Note 19 (Segments and Geographical Information) to the company’s consolidated financial statements. The company is now providing more detailed information regarding the geographic distribution of its long-term assets. This move is intended to align the company’s disclosures with prior filings and to provide greater transparency for investors about asset allocation and risk profiles across geographies.

Impact on Financial Position: Importantly, this update does not affect the company’s financial position for the periods presented. The amendment is purely for disclosure enhancement and does not reflect any change in the underlying assets, liabilities, or results of operations.

Update to Subsequent Events (Note 20): The amendment also updates Note 20 to reflect material subsequent events and corrects the number of ordinary shares outstanding as of May 30, 2026. This ensures that all outstanding share data is current, a detail that can influence market perceptions of dilution or potential corporate actions.

Updated Auditor Opinion and Certifications: The amendment includes a new opinion from the independent registered public accountants, Kost Forer Gabbay & Kasierer, to reflect the changes made solely with respect to Notes 19 and 20. Additionally, new certifications under Sections 302 and 906 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act have been filed, along with an updated auditor’s consent.

Stock and Warrants Information: The filing confirms that Class A Ordinary Shares and Warrants to purchase Class A Ordinary Shares remain listed on Nasdaq under the symbols PGY and PGYWW, respectively. As of the last business day of the company’s most recently completed second fiscal quarter (June 30, 2025), the public float was approximately \$1.11 billion, based on the closing price reported on Nasdaq.

Filing Status: Pagaya confirms it is a large accelerated filer and is not an emerging growth company or a smaller reporting company. The company has filed all required reports and is in compliance with electronic data submission requirements.

Key Investor Considerations and Potential Price-Sensitive Information

Increased Transparency on Asset Allocation: The more detailed breakdown of the company’s long-term assets by geography could impact investor perceptions of risk, especially if asset concentrations are revealed in higher-risk regions or sectors. This level of detail allows for a more accurate risk assessment and may influence institutional investor allocations.

Accurate Share Count and Dilution Risk: The update of shares outstanding to May 30, 2026, is essential for valuation models and for understanding potential dilution. Any significant changes in the share count or structure can directly affect share price.

Regulatory and Audit Assurance: The refreshed auditor opinion and certifications provide assurance of compliance and internal control, which is especially critical in today’s regulatory environment. There is no indication of material weaknesses or restatements, which is a net positive for shareholders.

No Correction of Material Errors: The company explicitly notes that no corrections to previously issued financial statements were required and that no restatements triggered the need for recovery analysis of incentive-based compensation.

Detailed Definitions and Corporate Structure Updates

The report includes clarified definitions of key terms and entities involved in Pagaya’s structure, partnerships, and financing activities, including “Financing Vehicles,” “PIPE Investment,” “EJF Investor,” and various share classes. These clarifications are crucial for understanding the company’s capitalization, governance, and partnership structures.

The company’s capital restructuring history, including the merger with EJF Acquisition Corp. and related PIPE investments, is explained in detail, providing context for recent changes in share structure and outstanding instruments.

Besi APac Sdn. Bhd., the Malaysian unit of top semiconductor assembly equipment manufacturer BE Semiconductor Industries N.V., has entered into a partnership with DHL Express by joining their GoGreen Plus programme. This programme aims to lower the emissions generated from Besi APac’s urgent global deliveries through the utilization of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). The partnership is projected to result in a reduction of over 400 tonnes in Well-to-Wheel (WTW) CO₂e emissions.

Reducing Emissions Through Responsible Practices

Besi APac is dedicated to the energy transition and acknowledges the importance of decreasing operational emissions through responsible business operations. Henk Jan Jonge Poerink, Managing Director of Besi APac and Senior Vice President of Global Operations at Besi N.V., stated that the company’s sustainability strategy extends to its supply chain activities. They are striving to incorporate environmental considerations into their procurement processes. SAF is seen as one of several methods that can assist in reducing aviation-related emissions. The company eagerly anticipates the opportunity to support the expansion of renewable alternatives.

Introduced in 2023, GoGreen Plus allows its clients to utilise SAF to decrease their indirect Scope 3 emissions, which arise from upstream and downstream transportation and distribution. This service is made possible through numerous SAF contracts that DHL has signed with its partners.

SAF, which is made from sustainable feedstocks like used cooking oil and other residues, can lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 80% compared to standard jet fuel. The ‘book & claim’ approach enables DHL to replace fossil fuels with sustainable fuels within its network directly and assign the associated lifecycle emission reductions to clients like Besi APac.

Besi APac’s Commitment to Sustainability

Besi APac’s subscription to GoGreen Plus is applicable across its international trade routes, covering major markets in the Asia Pacific, Europe, Americas, and Middle East. The initiative is aligned with the company’s 2025-2029 strategic plan, which includes minimising its environmental impact as a primary goal. Besi APac has significantly reduced its Scope 1 & 2 emission intensity ratio, fuel consumption intensity ratio, and increased electricity usage from renewable sources since 2019.

Alex Lee, Vice President of Commercial at DHL Express Malaysia, stated that DHL is committed to increasing the availability of emissions-reduced logistics solutions. Partnerships like this one showcase the practical application of this commitment.

DHL is one of the largest global users of SAF. The company increased the percentage of SAF in its own aircraft fleet to 10 percent in 2025, a significant increase from the 3.5 percent the previous year. DHL currently uses SAF at airports worldwide.

Questions & Answers

What is Besi APac’s strategy to reduce emissions in their operations?

Besi APac is committed to decreasing operational emissions through responsible business practices. This includes integrating environmental considerations into their procurement processes and using SAF to reduce aviation-related emissions.

How does DHL’s GoGreen Plus programme help to reduce emissions?

GoGreen Plus allows its customers to utilise SAF to reduce their indirect Scope 3 emissions arising from upstream and downstream transportation and distribution. It replaces fossil fuels with sustainable fuels within its network, attributing the associated emission reductions to its customers.

text:
The Board of Indian Oil Corporation (IndianOil) approved the formation of a 50:50 joint venture with M11 Energy Transition Private Limited to develop a 100 KTPA Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) based Sustainable Aviation Fuel plant at Paradip. The decision was taken at the company board meeting on 18 May 2026, and the project cost is estimated at Rs 10,636 million with a plus or minus thirty per cent tolerance. The proposal remains subject to statutory and Government approvals from NITI Aayog and DIPAM.

The project is intended to accelerate the development of sustainable and low-carbon aviation fuel and to bolster domestic energy security. IndianOil indicated that the plant will contribute to the company’s energy transition objectives and support decarbonisation efforts in the aviation sector. The initiative aligns with broader national policy to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from transport fuels.

Under the proposed structure, IndianOil and M11 Energy Transition will each hold fifty per cent of the equity in the Indian joint venture. The facility will use HEFA technology to convert vegetable oils and other suitable feedstocks into jet-grade fuel that meets regulatory specifications. Cost estimates include capital expenditure and commissioning costs and carry a contingency range reflecting market and feedstock uncertainties.

HEFA represents an established pathway for producing a drop in Sustainable Aviation Fuel from lipid feedstocks, and the Paradip site was selected for its logistical advantages. Proximity to feedstock sources and port facilities was cited as a factor in site selection, and the project has been designed to integrate with existing refinery operations and supply chains to optimise logistics. The design seeks to minimise additional transportation and handling.

IndianOil views the venture as part of its strategy to expand low-carbon fuel options and support the aviation industry's transition to cleaner fuels. Final investment decision and timelines will follow receipt of requisite approvals and completion of project studies. The company has positioned the plant as a step towards reducing reliance on fossil-based aviation fuels and enhancing capability in sustainable fuel production.

China’s Electrolyser Diplomacy, Path Dependency, and the Contest for Critical Energy Infrastructure in Latin America

China’s expanding role in Latin America’s green hydrogen sector extends well beyond trade and investment. Through the provision of electrolyser technology, proprietary telemetry systems, and state-backed financing conditioned on Chinese technical standards, Beijing is establishing path-dependent infrastructure lock-in across the region before the regulatory debate has begun. This paper examines the mechanism of that lock-in — from hardware compatibility to software dependency to ISO/IEC standard-setting — and traces the divergent exposure of Chile, which has anchored its hydrogen strategy to European certification requirements, against the greater vulnerability of Brazil and Argentina. The implications for European energy security and British post-Brexit strategy are direct and underexamined.

Energy as Critical Infrastructure: The 5G Precedent Revisited

The debate over Huawei’s role in European 5G networks was settled, eventually, on grounds that had little to do with price or technical performance. It was settled on the grounds of critical infrastructure security: the recognition that telecommunications networks are not commodity inputs but strategic assets whose architecture determines who can access, interrupt, or surveil the systems that modern societies depend upon. That recognition — resisted for years as protectionist overreach — is now embedded in EU and UK regulatory frameworks, as reflected in the European Commission’s 2019 Recommendation on Cybersecurity of 5G Networks and the UK Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021.

Energy infrastructure demands the same analytical framework. A hydrogen production facility is not a discrete industrial asset. It is a node in an evolving network of sensors, data flows, grid interactions, and contractual obligations. The telemetry systems embedded in Chinese electrolysers transmit operational data — production volumes, efficiency parameters, fault diagnostics — to remote management platforms. Where that data resides, who can access it, and what governs its use under the original financing agreement are not technical details. They are sovereignty questions.

Latin America is installing this infrastructure now, at scale, without the regulatory debate that preceded Europe’s 5G decisions. The difference in timing is not incidental: by the time the strategic implications become politically salient, the infrastructure will be in place, the contracts will be running, and the switching costs will have become prohibitive.

Energy is the new frontier of data sovereignty and strategic autonomy. The 5G debate established that critical infrastructure cannot be evaluated on price alone. Latin America has yet to apply that lesson to the sector that will define its economic trajectory for the next half-century.

The Mechanism of Lock-In: Path Dependency Beyond the Hardware

The concept of path dependency — developed in institutional economics to describe how early choices constrain future options — applies with particular force to technical infrastructure. The foundational works on this dynamic, including Paul A. David’s ‘Clio and the Economics of QWERTY’ (1985) and W. Brian Arthur’s ‘Competing Technologies, Increasing Returns, and Lock-In by Historical Events’ (1989), demonstrate that when a country adopts a specific technological standard for an initial installation, subsequent expansions face a structural incentive to maintain compatibility with that standard. The costs of switching — in engineering, procurement, retraining, and recertification — rise with each additional unit installed. The initial choice, however contingent, becomes progressively harder to reverse.

In the context of green hydrogen, this dynamic operates through three interlocking mechanisms. The first is hardware compatibility: electrolysers, compression systems, and storage units from different manufacturers are rarely interchangeable. Once a facility is built around Chinese equipment specifications, expansion units must either replicate those specifications or absorb significant integration costs. The second is software and telemetry dependency: the operational software controlling Chinese electrolysers is proprietary, and maintenance contracts — structured as conditions of the original financing agreements with Chinese state-backed lenders (as documented by the China-Latin America Finance Database, Global Development Policy Center, Boston University, 2024) — require continued engagement with the original supplier for updates, fault resolution, and performance certification. Switching the hardware without switching the software architecture is, in practice, rarely feasible.

The third mechanism is the most consequential and the least discussed: protocol standardisation within the network. As multiple facilities within a country or region adopt the same telemetry protocols, safety standards, and measurement methodologies — often because they share a common financier in the Export-Import Bank of China or the China Development Bank — a de facto technical ecosystem emerges. New entrants face the choice of adopting those protocols to ensure interoperability or accepting the costs of operating a parallel, incompatible system. This is path dependency at the network level: not a single facility locked into a vendor, but an entire national infrastructure locked into an architectural logic.

The lock-in is not in the hardware. It is in the maintenance contracts tied to state financing, the proprietary software that cannot be replaced without voiding warranty conditions, and the telemetry protocols that, once adopted at scale, become the de facto standard for the entire network.

Not a Monolithic Region: Chile, Brazil, and the Divergence of Exposure

The region’s exposure to Chinese technological lock-in varies significantly by country, and that variation is itself analytically instructive.

Chile represents the most strategically deliberate case. Santiago’s National Green Hydrogen Strategy, published in 2020 and revised in 2023, was designed with European market access as an explicit objective. The Port of Rotterdam agreement — under which Chilean green hydrogen exports are to be certified against EU standards for traceability and carbon intensity — has created a concrete regulatory incentive to maintain interoperability with European frameworks. Chilean authorities have been more selective in accepting Chinese financing arrangements that would impose incompatible certification requirements. This does not mean Chile is immune to path dependency dynamics — Chinese investment in Chilean renewable generation remains substantial — but Santiago entered negotiations with a clearer understanding of the downstream implications for market access.

Brazil and Argentina present a structurally different exposure profile. Neither country has established a comparable European market anchor for its hydrogen strategy. Brazil’s hydrogen ambitions are formidable — some projections place its potential share of the global market at ten per cent by 2050 — but the institutional framework for certification remains underdeveloped, and the urgency of securing financing for large-scale infrastructure projects has consistently outpaced the development of standards governance. The agreements signed during President Lula’s 2025 visit to Beijing — including the Envision Energy arrangement for sustainable aviation fuel and the Windey Energy Technology R&D partnership — were concluded in a context where the European alternative had not arrived at the negotiating table on equivalent terms. Argentina’s fiscal constraints amplify this dynamic: the turnkey model offered by Chinese state-backed financing — in which design, procurement, construction, and operational setup are bundled into a single integrated package — is structurally attractive to governments operating under severe liquidity constraints, precisely because it minimises the upfront institutional capacity required to manage the procurement process.

The divergence between Chile and its neighbours is not a function of geopolitical alignment or ideological preference. It is a function of institutional preparedness and the presence or absence of a concrete market anchor — a Rotterdam agreement, an EU certification partnership — that changes the calculus of which offer to accept.

Standard-Setting as Regulatory Power: The ISO/IEC Dimension

Behind the bilateral agreements and the financing packages, a less visible but more durable contest is under way in the technical committees of ISO, IEC, and the International Partnership for Hydrogen and Fuel Cells in the Economy (IPHE). These bodies set the international norms that define what green hydrogen is, how it is measured, and under what conditions it can be traded across borders. In a nascent market, first-mover advantage in standard-setting translates directly into long-term market access conditions.

China has invested systematically in this terrain. The International Hydrogen Energy Centre (IHEC), established with UNIDO in 2021, provides an institutional platform for Chinese standard proposals to enter multilateral technical negotiations with the imprimatur of a UN-affiliated body. The certification frameworks embedded in the China-CELAC Ministerial Forum agreements of May 2025 are not merely bilateral conveniences: they are pilot implementations of Chinese standard proposals that, if adopted widely across the region, will generate precisely the network-level path dependency described above — this time at the inter-governmental rather than the facility level.

For Latin American countries that aspire to export to European markets, the implications are direct. The EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and the hydrogen-specific additionality, temporal correlation, and geographic correlation requirements under the Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/1185 on renewable fuels of non-biological origin establish a demanding certification regime. A country whose production infrastructure was designed and certified against Chinese standards will face non-trivial adaptation costs to meet European requirements — costs that will be borne at a moment when the installed base is already substantial and the contractual obligations of the original financing are still running.

The European and British Calculus

For policymakers in Brussels and London, the situation in Latin America is neither peripheral nor merely humanitarian in its implications. It bears directly on their own energy security calculations.

Europe’s REPowerEU targets and the UK’s Hydrogen Strategy both depend, at the margin, on imports from regions with high renewable potential. Latin America — particularly Brazil, Chile, and the Andean corridor — features in the supply diversification scenarios of every serious European energy planning document. Supply diversification is only as meaningful, however, as the technical and political reliability of the supply chain. A Latin American hydrogen sector built on Chinese standards, Chinese telemetry, and Chinese financing agreements introduces a layer of systemic dependency that complicates the risk calculus for European offtakers and regulators.

The United Kingdom has instruments it has not fully deployed. British International Investment (BII) has the mandate and the balance sheet to compete for infrastructure financing in Latin America. UK Export Finance has supported energy transition projects in comparable markets. The British Standards Institution has the technical credibility to anchor a standards cooperation partnership. What has been absent is the strategic coherence to bundle these instruments into a proposition that competes with China’s integrated offer — financing, technology, certification, and implementation — in terms that Latin American governments find credible. COP30 in Belém was the most recent moment at which that proposition could have been advanced. It was not.

Conclusion: Sovereignty Requires a Standards Architecture

The green hydrogen sector in Latin America is at an early stage of infrastructure consolidation. Path dependency is not yet irreversible. The window for deliberate institutional action — on certification standards, on financing conditionalities, on telemetry governance — remains open. It will not remain open indefinitely.

The policy implication is not to reject Chinese capital. Latin America needs investment at a scale and speed that its Western partners have not matched. The implication is more precise: to condition the terms on which that capital is accepted. Specifically, to insist — at the level of national regulation and, where possible, at the level of a coordinated regional framework — that financing arrangements do not impose proprietary technical standards that foreclose future interoperability with European certification requirements.

Chile has demonstrated, partially, that this is achievable: the Rotterdam anchor provides a regulatory reference point that changes the negotiating dynamic. Brazil, Argentina, and Colombia require comparable anchors — whether through bilateral certification agreements with the EU, through the Inter-American Development Bank’s standards governance work, or through the construction of a regional hydrogen certification body with genuine technical authority.

The energy transition is not only a climate project. It is a redistribution of technological power. In Latin America, the terms of that redistribution are being set now, in procurement decisions, financing agreements, and technical standards negotiations that attract far less political attention than they warrant. The infrastructure being installed today will determine the region’s strategic options for decades. A transition that is green but not sovereign is not, in any meaningful sense, a transition at all.
